Article abstract-A 57-year-old woman without a known neoplasia devel- 
oped opsoclonus, myoclonus, and ataxia. Positive anti-Ri antibodies were 
present in both serum and CSF. The patient also had progressive 
encephalomyelitis with rigidity, an association not previously described. 
NEUROLOGY 1994;44:1521-1522 
Antineuronal autoantibodies, present in serum 
and CSF in patients with some paraneoplastic syn- 
dromes, are usually predictive of occult tumor.1 
Anti-Ri antibodies have been identified in women 
with ataxia and opsoclonus and breast cancer., 
However, the full spectrum of neurologic manifes- 
tations in patients with anti-Ri antibodies is 
unclear: as is whether the antibodies may be pres- 
ent in patients without t~rnor.~,~ We present a 
patient with opsoclonus, myoclonus, ataxia, and 
positive anti-Ri antibodies in both serum and CSF 
who later developed a progressive encephalomyeli- 
tis with rigidity (PEM). Although a gynecologic 
occult cancer was suspected, an extensive evalua- 
tion was repeatedly negative. 
Case report. A 57-year-old woman was evaluated in 
March 1992 because of a 4-month history of progressive 
gait instability. In January 1992, she was unable to 
walk unaided. One month later, she developed vertigo, 
diplopia, and oscillopsia. Her family noticed continuous 
and involuntary movements of her eyes. She also had 
sudden involuntary movements in the four limbs, easily 
evoked by voluntary movements. Medical history was 
unremarkable except for a cerebral infarct in 1983 that 
left her with a minimal left hemiparesis. CT done at the 
time of the infarct was normal. Percutaneous angiogra- 
phy was interpreted as fibromuscular dysplasia of the 
right internal carotid artery. 
General physical examination was normal. On neuro- 
logic examination, cognition was normal. There was a 
mild residual left spastic hemiparesis and the left plan- 
tar response was extensor. Sensory examination was nor- 
mal. There were involuntary, chaotic, multidirectional 
saccadic ocular movements in all directions of gaze. The 
movements persisted when the patient’s eyes were closed 
or during sleep, and were markedly exacerbated by 
attempted pursuit or refixation and by stress. She had 
asynchronous myoclonus of the face, tongue, and palate 
and continuous asymmetric, arrhythmic myoclonic activ- 
ity of all limbs, mainly proximal, which disappeared with 
total resting or during sleep. Myoclonus was easily elicit- 
ed by gentle touch and startle; sometimes, the move- 
ments were massive and synchronous in all limbs. She 
had severe truncal instability and severe gait ataxia that 
prevented her from walking unassisted. 
Routine laboratory and immunologic analysis, serum 
carcinoembryonic antigen, and CA125 were normal. CSF 
contained 16 mononuclear WBC/mm3 (90% lymphocytes), 
with normal protein and glucose levels and negative 
cytologic examination. Serology for syphilis, borrelia, 
mycoplasma, influenza, coxsackie, mumps, adenovirus, 
measles, varicella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex 
virus, and Epstein-Barr virus was negative in both plas- 
ma and CSF. Cranial MRI showed a right ventral pon- 
tine lesion with low-signal intensity on TI-weighted 
images that did not enhance after gadolinium adminis-

tration, and high-signal intensity on T,-weighted images. 
CTs of the head, thorax, and abdomen, gastrointestinal 
evaluation, mammograms, bone scan, thyroid isotopic 
studies, and exploratory laparotomy with biopsy of both 
ovaries were normal or negative. 
By an avidin-biotin peroxidase technique, serum and 
CSF reacted with the nucleus and, to lesser degree, with 
the cytoplasm of neurons of different areas of the CNS, 
but not with the sensory neurons of the dorsal root gan- 
glia. In immunoblots of cortical neuron extracts, serum 
and CSF reacted with protein antigens of 80 kd and 55 
kd of apparent molecular mass.2 The titer in serum was 
1:40,000, and in CSF it was 1:400. CSF IgG index was 
1.20. The anti-Ri index defined by the formula [CSF anti- 
Ri titer/serum anti-Ri:CSF IgG/serum IgG] was 1.5 
(upper normal value, 11, consistent with intrathecal syn- 
thesis of the antib~dy.~ 
The myoclonus and opsoclonus responded partially to 
thiamine hydrochloride (100 mgld) and increasing doses 
of clonazepam (up to 1 mg t.i.d.1. Thiamine hydrochloride 
was stopped and prednisone (60 mgld) was introduced 20 
days later with better results, but 3 weeks later the 
patient returned to initial status. Clonazepam was then 
tapered and replaced by triazolam (0.06 mg), with pro- 
gressive disappearance of opsoclonus and myoclonus. 
Two months later, she presented with progressive parox- 
ysms of intense, painful muscle spasm in both the 
paraspinal and left limb muscles, with flexion of the 
upper limb and extension of the lower limb, associated 
with piloerection, hyperventilation, choking sensation, 
flushing of the face, and profuse sweating. Fever or 
changes in blood pressure were not observed. These 
episodes lasted from minutes to several hours and were 
relieved by parenteral administration of diazepam. They 
were precipitated by emotional distress, startle, light 
cutaneous stimuli, and even normal conversation. 
Rigidity and spasms were severe and produced a left hip 
fracture. Baclofen was started (10 mg b.i.d.1 with steady 
improvement. 
August 1994 NEUROLOGY 44 1521

In July, prednisone and triazolam were discontinued 
and the opsoclonus recurred. Drugs were restarted with 
steady improvement of the opsoclonus, rigidity, and 
painful muscle spasms. By January 1993, eye move- 
ments were normal and the patient was able to walk 
with a walker and to use the left upper limb when driv- 
ing her wheel-chair. A new extensive work-up including 
a needle biopsy of several small breast nodules was nega- 
tive. Triazolam was discontinued and prednisone tapered 
to 20 mg/d. The patient remained stable until June 1993, 
when she died from a pulmonary thromboembolism. 
Permission for autopsy was denied.
